newsitem.title: UK: UK output prices show pipeline inflation still low.
newsitem.headline: UK output prices show pipeline inflation still low.

text.p: A modest rise in British factory gate prices in October showed pipeline inflationary pressures remained subdued, economists said on Monday.
But higher fuel and oil prices continued to put upward pressure on input prices and threaten retail price inflation in the coming months as they feed through to the petrol pump.

Economists said Bank of England Governor Eddie George was unlikely to use the supply-side push from higher oil prices to fuel his call for a rise in interest rates, as he will recognise them as a purely temporary phenomenon.

UK output prices rose 0.2 percent in October on the previous month giving a 2.3 percent year-on-year rise. Seasonally adjusted input prices rose 0.5 percent on the month and fell 2.0 percent on the year.

"All of the rise (in input prices) in October was due to higher fuel and oil prices -- all of the other components were either flat or fell, suggesting that, oil apart, commodity prices remain subdued," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
Crude oil prices rose 6.8 percent in October versus September, giving a massive 44.3 percent annual rise. Core output price inflation stuck to its 30-year low of 0.9 percent.
Economists said the hefty rise in crude oil prices was bound to feed through to the retail level in the coming months in the form of higher petrol prices.
"They will push up RPI over the next few months, but rather that than a general pick-up in raw material cost pressures," said Loynes.

John Shepperd, economist at Yamaichi International Europe, said the figures would be unlikely to add weight to George's calls for higher interest rates. "George will look at these figures with some degree of satisfaction. They are unlikely to change his view on the next move on interest rates," he said.
General Accident economist Andrew Milligan said the figures would dampen wilder speculation of an early rate rise because of the weak core output price data.

"There's little reason to think RPIX, excluding the impact of higher oil prices, is going to show a marked upward jump in the coming months. It's still quite possible that we'll see the core rate dip back below three percent," he said.
He said if Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke could fend off calls for a rate rise until the beginning of next year, he may well have a better set of inflation numbers to argue his corner.
Economists said the dampening impact of sterling's recent appreciation would be felt to a greater extent next month.
"The input price side was a little surprising -- we had expected the rise in sterling to have dampened the oil price effect," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist James Barty.
"By the time we get to next month's figures, I think the worst of the oil price rise will have come through and we'll see the positive effects from the rise in sterling."
Sterling rose 4.5 percent against the dollar in October, versus a 6.8 percent monthly rise in crude oil prices.
Analysts said time lags and currency hedging operations by companies which use oil products weakened the impact of sterling's rise on the cost of buying crude oil.
"Companies plan their supply schedules some time in advance, so it will clearly take some time for the full impact of price increases to feed through," said General Accident's Milligan.
He added that not all price increases would be passed along the supply chain immediately.
